A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same five-RCT targeting study. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained analyses can be matched despite reorganization and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original analyses of treatment-effect heterogeneity and targeting welfare using five existing RCT datasets, including simulated confounding and appendix budget experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical analyses and adds feature-only targeting evaluations, welfare comparisons, and budget sensitivity results.

M1.justification: v2 adds a feature-only targeting procedure that trains a second-stage random forest on cross-fitted pseudo-outcome differences and predicts effects for evaluation individuals (Appendix A.1). The outcome-informed ranking underlying the earlier analysis remains separately as the semi-synthetic procedure. This substantially changes how targeting scores are obtained.

E1.justification: Both versions use TUP, NSW, postoperative pain, acupuncture, and STAR, with the same populations, interventions, and outcome tasks. The added feature-only experiments change estimation and evaluation procedures within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding policy comparisons retain treatment-effect targeting, risk-based targeting, and uniformly random allocation. No additional baseline strategy is introduced; the feature-only treatment-effect implementation is the methodological expansion.

E3.justification: The new real-setting evaluation reserves a separate evaluation split and performs nuisance-model cross-fitting within the training split (Appendix A.1). This is distinguished from the outcome-informed, two-way cross-fitted semi-synthetic evaluation. The confounding-removal rule, welfare objectives, and existing 30%/40% budget settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds an analysis contrasting feature-based prediction with direct pseudo-outcome ranking to investigate learnability separately from confounding. Appendix A.4.1 and A.4.3 extend welfare-function and budget sensitivity analyses to the feature-only procedure; the earlier outcome-informed budget analyses remain in A.4.2.

E5.justification: Equation (5) changes the confidence-interval variance numerator from squared kernel weights in v1 to unsquared weights in v2. Figure 1's plotted intervals remain identical, establishing a formula-reporting change without demonstrating recalculation. Neither version supplies repeated-run counts or seeds.

E6.justification: New Figure 2 and Table II report mixed feature-only targeting performance, including alpha thresholds of zero throughout the TUP and postoperative-pain rows. These are additional conditions, not same-setting performance declines. Table I also revises thresholds: TUP at 10% removal changes from 8 to 8.5, and postoperative pain at 5% changes from 7.5 to 'na'.

T1.justification: The potential-outcome assumptions, doubly robust estimator, and policy-value decomposition are retained. Equation (5) changes mathematically through removal of the kernel-weight square. The general parameterized power-mean definition is also omitted in favor of the welfare special cases; no new theorem or proof appears.

C1.justification: v1 broadly concludes that even biased treatment-effect targeting is almost always preferable. v2 makes this advantage conditional on accurate effect estimation, explicitly acknowledges that most examined RCTs do not support such prediction, and redirects its recommendation toward better data collection and modeling.

C2.justification: v2 identifies prediction reliability as a central bottleneck, interprets overlapping confidence intervals more cautiously, and explains that direct pseudo-outcome ranking uses unavailable future information. Its conclusion also adds a substantive applicability limit: non-consequentialist preferences may justify targeting vulnerability directly.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.1 supplies essential construction details for both experimental regimes: split organization, nuisance-model cross-fitting, second-stage random-forest prediction, and averaging nuisance estimates for evaluation. This substantially improves documentation of how targeting and evaluation scores are produced, although hyperparameters and software details remain sparse.

R1.justification: v2 adds Gupta et al. on theoretical targeting guarantees, Haushofer et al. on impact versus deprivation, Kube et al. on allocation preferences, and Vickers et al. for the acupuncture trial. These modestly broaden positioning and attribution without replacing the existing related-work framework.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements, results discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around prediction reliability. Related work becomes part of the introduction, methods are condensed and reorganized, and kernel-smoothing mathematics moves to Appendix A.3 alongside a more structured experimental appendix.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figure 2, Table II, and extensive feature-only appendix plots. The earlier Figure 2 becomes Figure 3 with revised axis scales and an explicit outcome-informed caption; earlier budget Figures 3–7 correspond to Figures 9–13. Figure 1's plotted content is retained.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves a central weakness in v1's practical recommendation by distinguishing outcome-informed ranking from deployable feature-only prediction. New held-out evaluations and appendix analyses reveal limited practical gains, and the abstract and conclusion are narrowed accordingly. This substantially strengthens the connection between evidence and policy advice. The unexplained confidence-interval formula change remains a reporting weakness, but does not outweigh that improvement.
